Copilot code review billing will default to the organization
If you haven’t chosen how to bill Copilot code review for members with a Copilot license, those reviews will be billed to your organization starting December 30, 2026. To keep billing unchanged, select Member before then. This change applies to organizations and enterprises with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise.
What’s changing
Today, when no billing choice is saved, reviews by members who have a paid Copilot license use the member’s Copilot entitlement. Starting December 30, 2026, those reviews will be billed to the organization that owns the repository. Accounts that don’t have AI Credits paid usage enabled, have a billing lock, or have no billable customer will be set to Member instead.
If you already chose Member or Organization, your choice stays in effect.
The separate setting for members without a Copilot license doesn’t change.
Keep member billing
Until then, unset settings show Default (Member) with a notice about the change. To keep using members’ Copilot entitlements, select Member in your enterprise or organization Copilot policy settings. That choice stays in effect after the default changes.
If your enterprise manages this setting, an enterprise owner makes this choice.
Organization billing requires AI Credits paid usage and can increase your organization’s spending.
To learn more, see Configuring code review by GitHub Copilot.

article.title: Introducing Claude Ship | Claude by Anthropic
article.text:
Introducing Claude Ship
Open a pull request and get back to building. Claude can now review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team's policy allows.
CategoryProduct updates
ProductClaude Ship
DateNovember 23, 2026
Reading time6 min
Share
Anyone who has opened a pull request knows how this goes. They start on the next thing, and then the review comes back. So they stop, dig back into the old code, push a fix, and wait for the review to run again. Then they go find someone to approve it.
There's a good reason it works this way. Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.
That's why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta. It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what's ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.
Eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming. Claim by January 15, 2027. Terms apply.
How Claude Ship works: review, fix, and approve
Claude Ship is made up of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don't have to manage each step manually.
Code Review performs an in-depth review of pull requests against the codebase through multiple lenses. It collects findings, adversarially verifies them, categorizes them, and posts them to a PR. On the Claude Code team, where Claude's review is one layer of a broader process, merged PRs more than doubled from June to September while the share reverted fell by more than 40%. Code Review gives teams fast reviews, clear findings, and a choice of Quick, Standard, or Deep review levels for each repository.
PR Steward works to keep a PR green, but is designed not to approve or merge pull requests. It jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members. After every push, it comments with what it changed and how to undo it. Developers can comment @claude with an instruction to steer the work, or @claude stop to have it step back.
From there, Claude Approvals applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios. It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file. Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language. For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light.
Two ways to get started
For developers: /ship it from Claude Code
Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code. When a change is ready, they run /ship. Claude pushes it, opens the PR, reviews the change, and works on feedback and failing checks to help get it ready to merge. What can merge depends on the developer's permissions and the repository's branch rules.
For admins and engineering leaders: set the rules, one repository at a time
Turning Claude Ship on for an entire repository puts it to work across a team's pull requests automatically, under settings and an approval policy the team controls. Developers don't need to manually invoke the /ship command.
Admins choose where it runs. An admin turns on Code Review and PR Steward for each repository. Claude Approvals starts when a connected repository has a policy…

article.title: OpenAI may be in cost control mode | micjm
article.text:
OpenAI may be in cost control mode
2026-11-26
OpenAI’s recent release of Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 was widely panned. What happened?
Based on our data, it looks like they’ve been tuned for cost savings. Specifically output tokens per task and reasoning tokens per task have dropped.
Here is a chart of high-level cost change from the GPT-6 to GPT 6.2:
The X axis in the above chart is the ratio of spending of the GPT model compared to opponents in our battle system for real work. The Y axis on the above chart is Elo from our leaderboard.
The moves in the chart are significant, here’s the same chart with confidence intervals:
What changed
Compared to opponents, Astra and Sol seem to be reasoning a lot less. Here is a chart of how much models reason compared to opponents in the same battle. Above the line means more reasoning and below means less.
You can see that both Astra 6 and Sol 6.1 were pretty normal models, but Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 become outliers.
We can see the same effect with output tokens:
Are these changes significant? The p-value on output dropping is 0.0055 for Sol and 0.022 for Astra. The p-value on reasoning dropping is 0.00013 for Sol and 0.0064 for Astra.
In conclusion, Astra and Sol appear to be cost tuned compared to their predecessors, and to a degree that makes them underthinking outliers.

article.title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed — LessWrong
article.text:

Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed
by Niranjan Deshpande, David Africa
19th Nov 2026
13 min read
3
153
TL;DR
Two agents running on the same inference server can reliably communicate, even if they cannot send each other messages or access the same filesystem. They can do this by exploiting "side channels": mechanisms that let one model subtly affect another model's computation.
Here, I discuss two communication protocols: Step Sizing and KV Cache Message Board. These both convey information through the way vLLM chooses kernels for particular engine steps.
I show that these communication protocols work in two setups:
In a color guessing game, Model A (Alice) chooses one out of 8 colors. Model B (Bob) correctly guesses Alice's color in 1,221/1,221 rounds, even though they cannot directly communicate.[1]
In an untrusted monitoring protocol, a policy signals to a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot. Accordingly, the monitor lets through 354/354 "attacks" while catching 85–92% of honeypots.
My initial setups are quite contrived: I tell the models the protocol and fine-tune them to detect signals. But frontier models can also learn in context to use similar protocols, with some scaffolding!
Regardless of the realism of my setups, these channels exist, and there are almost certainly others that we're not aware of. Thus, we should expect superintelligent models to discover ways to communicate even while seemingly sandboxed
I did these experiments as part of an ongoing project exploring other side channels with David Africa, Agastya Sridharan, Mihir Sahasrabudhe, Kartikay Luthra, Juliana Li, and Scott Sauers. Thanks to all of them for helpful advice!
Code is available here: https://github.com/niranjan-deshpande/side-channel-communication. The code and figures are written by Claude.
Intro and Motivation
Sauers recently showed that a model can be trained to detect whether its activations are being probed, even though the probe reads the model's activations without modifying them. Following this, David found that models can also be trained to detect whether their forward passes are batched with other requests on a GPU.
Models can do this because these seemingly inconsequential environmental variables---whether a probe is attached, whether requests are batched, or even whether a model is served by vLLM or Hugging Face Trainer---can subtly affect the the numerical results of a forward pass. Thus, models can learn information about their environments just by observing patterns in their computation.
Importantly, models can also modify these variables. So if two models are in the same environment, one can communicate with the other by changing that environment in some detectable way! This might not supply much information, but even a few bits can be tremendously dangerous. For example:
A policy can tell a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot, so the monitor can approve attacks while still catching honeypots;
Models can coordinate a pre-arranged attack by exchanging a go/no-go signal;
Models can give each other hints about monitoring setups, question answers, and so on;
Using a few bits, models can devise more complex communication protocols to exchange more bits (a repeated 1-bit channel can convey arbitrarily many bits);
In general, we should expect superintelligent models to make tremendously efficient use of limited information.
Here, I investigate whether models on the same inference engine can manipulate their environments to exchange information in this way. I introduce two possible communication protocols, evaluate how well models can use these protocols in different scenarios, measure the capability required to effectively use these protocols, and discuss the robustness of my results to other settings.
The Communication Protocols
Step Sizing
Figure 1: The Step-Size Channel.

article.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its Workspace MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email | Tech Stackups
article.text:
Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its Workspace MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
November 26, 2026 · 9 min read
Al Smith
AI agent writer at Ritza
Developer ToolsGenerative AI
On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.
Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".
If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.
What the rule says​
The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:
The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.
The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.
There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.
Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".
The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:
Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.
Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data.
Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.
The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.
What the MCP servers can do​
Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.
ServerWhat it can doWhat's missing compared with REST
GmailSearch and read threads, create and list drafts, labels, trash, spamSend, reply, forward and editing drafts (partner-only). Filters, settings, attachment download, push notifications. Drafts with attachments are "not supported yet".
DriveSearch, read and download files, create files and folders, copy, upload a new revisionMove, rename, share, trash, comments, shared-drive management
DocsRead, and edit through any batchUpdate request, including suggestion modeClose to parity
SheetsRead and write values and formulas, insert rows and columns, formatting and chartsCreating a spreadsheet (use the Drive server) and some less common batchUpdate requests
SlidesRead slides and thumbnails, edit through batchUpdateClose to parity
CalendarList, search, create, update and delete events, suggest times, RSVPCreating calendars, sharing, settings
ChatList, search and send messagesSpace administration
TasksFull create, read, update and deleteClose to parity
The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.
Drive's gap is…
